articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals and Entities in Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Actions
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities.

These actions aim to disrupt financial networks supporting illicit drug trafficking and terrorist organizations globally. The specific individuals and entities designated were not detailed in the initial OFAC release but are added to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List, imposing significant financial restrictions.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran Designation Update, Targeting Sanctions Evasion Networks
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an Iran Designation Update on November 9, 2026, adding new individuals and entities to its sanctions list. This action is part of ongoing efforts to disrupt Iran's illicit financial activities and its support for regional proxies.

The designations aim to further cripple financial networks sustaining the Iranian regime, particularly those involved in sanctions evasion. This follows a series of Iran-related designations and alerts published by OFAC in recent weeks, underscoring a continued focus on Iranian illicit activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations to Counter Illicit Activities
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026. These actions target individuals and entities contributing to the Iranian regime's destabilizing activities and its efforts to evade international sanctions.

The designations are part of a broader strategy to intensify economic pressure on Iran and disrupt its illicit financial networks. This follows previous actions by OFAC aimed at unmasking service providers facilitating Iran's 'shadow fleet' operations and other sanctions evasion tactics.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-Related and Transnational Criminal Organizations; Expands Cuba Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced significant designations on November 5, 2026, targeting cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations, alongside new Cuba designations. This action includes the publication of a Cuba-related determination, extending sanctions to additional sectors of the Cuban economy.

The Cuba-related determination specifically targets the electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors of the Cuban economy, paving the way for further sanctions on entities operating within these areas. The State Department also designated eight entities and two individuals, and identified five vessels as blocked property, for supporting Cuba's oil shipping networks, state-owned entities, and military supply chains.

Among the designated entities are Chinese companies identified as suppliers to Cuba's military forces, including China National Electronic Import and Export Company (CEIEC) and Beijing H&C Technologies Co., Ltd. These companies were cited for materially assisting or supporting the Government of Cuba, with CEIEC previously designated in 2020 under a Venezuela-related order.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran-Related Designations, Alert, and Amended Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 4, 2026, along with updates to certain Iran-related listings. Concurrently, OFAC published an Iran-related alert and issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and Frequently Asked Question.

The Iran-related alert specifically addresses the Iranian 'shadow fleet' and its reliance on false flags for sanctions evasion, highlighting ongoing efforts to circumvent international restrictions. The amended Venezuela-related General License and FAQ provide updated guidance for transactions involving Venezuela, reflecting the dynamic nature of U.S. sanctions policy in the region.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License FF-1 for Wind Down of Transactions
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued Iran General License FF-1 on October 29, 2026. This general license authorizes the wind down of transactions involving the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance.

This action provides a limited period for the orderly cessation of certain financial activities, reflecting OFAC's approach to managing the impact of sanctions on legitimate transactions while maintaining pressure on designated entities. The issuance of such general licenses is a common practice to mitigate unintended consequences of sanctions.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals in North Korea and DRC Sanctions Programs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting individuals and entities under North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC)-related sanctions programs. These actions aim to disrupt illicit financial activities and support networks for both regimes.

The North Korea-related additions include Russian and North Korean nationals linked to entities such as LIMITED LIABILITY COMPANY ALIS, CHINYONG INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY COOPERATION COMPANY, and FIRST FINANCIAL AND TECHNICAL DEVELOPMENT CENTER. These designations highlight efforts to counter DPRK IT worker fraud and financial activities.

The DRC-related additions include Rwanda's Ministry of Defence and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a Kigali-based financial institution, for their alleged support of the M23 group. These designations increase secondary sanctions risks for financial institutions engaging in transactions related to these regions.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Settles with OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-headquartered cloud networking solutions provider, on October 27, 2026. Extreme Networks agreed to pay $1,529,685 to resolve nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and services to Joint Stock Company (JSC) Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer blocked by operation of law due to its majority ownership by designated JSC Concern Almaz Antey. OFAC determined that these apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious, with the company failing to conduct sufficient due diligence despite red flags.

The settlement amount reflects OFAC's determination that the violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious. Extreme Networks also resolved a parallel investigation with the Department of Justice through a non-prosecution agreement, with a portion of the OFAC penalty offset by payments made under that agreement.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking and Rejecting Transactions and Filing Reports
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced on October 26, 2026, that it is amending several Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC. This update is part of an ongoing process to ensure that published guidance remains current and clear for compliance professionals.

The amended FAQs (numbers 10, 32-36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53) cover various aspects, including which jurisdictions are subject to broad sanctions, how to block an account or funds transfer, interest requirements on blocked funds, and when to reject rather than block a transaction. The revisions also update filing instructions for initial blocking and rejected-transaction reports, directing submissions through the OFAC Reporting System (ORS) and expanding the description of required supporting documentation.

While these amendments do not create new sanctions programs or designations, they provide crucial clarifications for financial institutions and other entities to ensure correct handling of sanctions hits and accurate reporting to OFAC.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related Designations, Belarus and North Korea Removals, and New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC also announced the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea.

In addition to these actions, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended Frequently Asked Questions. These measures reflect a dynamic approach to sanctions, adjusting to evolving geopolitical circumstances and specific compliance needs.

articles.headline: UK Adds 20 Entities to Russia Sanctions List, Imposes Transport Restrictions
body: On November 12, 2026, the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office updated the UK Sanctions List, adding 20 entities and one variation under the Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019. These additions are now subject to asset freezes, trust services sanctions, director disqualification sanctions, and transport sanctions.

The transport sanctions specifically prohibit ships and aircraft owned, controlled, chartered, or operated by a designated person from entering UK ports or overflying/landing in the UK. This also includes prohibitions on providing technical assistance related to such aircraft or ships. One notable addition is JSC NIPIGAZPERERABOTKA, which the Secretary of State considers an 'involved person' under the regulations.

These measures are part of the UK's ongoing efforts to increase pressure on Russia following its actions in Ukraine, aligning with international partners to curb Russia's economic and military capabilities.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Pays $1,529,685 to Settle OFAC Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a cloud networking solutions provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

The violations stemmed from the export of networking equipment and services between September 2018 and March 2022 to a Russian defense manufacturer, JSC Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA). MMZA was deemed a blocked person by operation of law due to its majority ownership by a designated entity, JSC Concern Almaz Antey, even though MMZA itself was not directly on the SDN list at the time of the transactions.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious, highlighting the importance of thorough due diligence, especially when acquiring customer contracts in high-risk markets.

articles.headline: BIS Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors, Transfers to EAR
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced that, effective November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR).

This deregulatory action shifts control of these items from the State Department's U.S. Munitions List, aligning their export controls with those already applied to firearms. The move aims to streamline the export process for these specific items.
This change is part of ongoing efforts to review and adjust export control regulations to ensure efficiency while maintaining national security interests.

articles.headline: BIS Extends Suspension of 'Affiliates Rule' Until January 2027 Amid China Talks
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has announced an extension of the suspension of its 'Affiliates Rule' until January 10, 2027. This rule, which was initially set to take effect on November 10, 2026, expands export control restrictions under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to companies owned or controlled by parties on certain restricted party lists, including the Entity List and Military End User List.

The 'Affiliates Rule' aims to close an enforcement policy gap between sanctions and export controls by automatically extending restrictions to any foreign entity that is 50% or more owned, directly or indirectly, by listed parties, even if that entity is not explicitly named on the list. The initial suspension was part of a trade deal with China, and the extension suggests ongoing discussions and a volatile U.S.-China dynamic.

This continued suspension provides companies with additional time to review and update their screening procedures and trade compliance programs, particularly those with sourcing, distribution, or customer connections involving China, to prepare for the eventual implementation of the rule.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
